utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I understand counsel for Mr. Milan Simic has a submission to make. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. I was just informed that my client hasn't come and that he is not feeling well, and I established a telephone connection with him just a few minutes ago and he waived his right to be present today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. So we can proceed, Mr. di Fazio. Oh, it's Mr. Weiner. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning. Just very briefly. I just want to quickly address three issues on the amendments and let you know where the Prosecution is heading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: With regard to the date relating to Simo Zaric, the final date of December 31st, 1992, as opposed to at least two other defendants having their final date of December 31st, 1993, we've spoken to -- we've researched the issue, we've even talked to Defence counsel, and apparently that was part of an agreement between Defence counsel and Prosecution some years ago, based on Mr. Zaric's role, and they decided to use the December 31st, 1992 date. So we are going to stay with the date which was part of discussions between Mr. Pisarevic and Prosecutor Nancy Paterson some years ago. With regard to the second issue that was raised yesterday, the use of the terms "wanton" and "excessive," we examined the Bosnian/Serbian/Croatian, or the indictments in Bosnian and Serbo-Croatian, and we noticed that in those indictments Articles -- paragraphs 14(e), 15(f), 17(e) and 18(f), they don't use the terms either "wanton" or "excessive," unlike the English versions. What we would like to do today, to make this much easier, is provide the language, potential language that we could amend the paragraphs to, to at least the Court today, let it be translated, if you want it to call it the draft language, let it be translated into B/C/S, let it be shown by counsel, at least today, to the defendants before all counsel leave on holiday, and by Monday we will make a decision. Since the treaties or the conventions use different terminology - I believe grave breaches does not use the term "wanton" -- grave breaches does use the term "wanton," some of the other treaties or conventions do not use the term "wanton," we would like to run this by our appellate decision, because this is an issue for not only our case, but other cases within the Tribunal, and come to some agreement as to where we would be heading. So what we would like to do, we thought, to facilitate this, provide all the language to the Registry today, let them get it translated, or we could even translate the words "wanton" and "excessive," provide it in draft form, let counsel discuss it with their clients, and by Monday we would have a decision. That way they can still respond to it, in any manner that they would like, on Tuesday or Wednesday. But we would -- that way we could facilitate and keep this moving as opposed to making our filing on Monday and then they would have to show it to their clients, and that would further delay this hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So that discussion that you're going to have with the Defence counsel is to make them understand what the language of our amendment will include --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- in those paragraphs which you are asking to be part of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. What we'll do is we'll give them the potential language, and if we decide to make that change on Monday, they will at least have had the opportunity today to notify their clients and discuss it with their clients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I just want to make it clear that while the international instruments may have the language that they have on those instruments, the interpretation is what the Prosecutor would like to make, according to the evidence that they have, perhaps, maybe, because this use of the word "wanton," for instance, or "excessive destruction," it depends on the type of evidence you have. All right, the Trial Chamber will leave that to the parties to deal with but making sure that it doesn't encroach upon the time given to the Defence counsel to file their written submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's why we want to get it to them today so -- we do not delay this and they can just start looking at that, consider it, review it and work on their submissions immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. di Fazio, we'll continue with the witness who is still on -- under solemn declaration. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Witness, I won't trouble you with documents too much today bearing in mind the recent difficulties you've had with your eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is everything fine with the accused? Can they understand the interpretation? All right. Yeah, we can proceed. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Witness, I want to ask you about some aspects of life for civilians who were not incarcerated in Bosanski Samac in the period of time between April and August and September of 1992. You have briefly mentioned curfews. Were curfews or was a curfew established in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: From when was it imposed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the beginning of the war, of war events in the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you remember how you became aware of it, the existence of the curfew?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the media, Radio Samac, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did the curfew apply to all citizens?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was a reason ever given for the imposition of a curfew?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever see anyone or any groups of people not obeying the curfew?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the time that you were in Bosanski Samac prior to your arrest, was there any prohibition against the gathering of people into groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who did that apply to, what people did that apply to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How did you find out about that prohibition against the gathering into groups of Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were posters all over the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And thinking back now, bearing in mind the events of the night of the 16th and 17th of April, about how much longer after that, that night, did that prohibition against the gathering into groups start?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe some ten days after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you take care to avoid congregating with Muslims or Croats into -- in groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Following the events of the nights of the 16th and 17th of April, was there any requirement as to dress that how you had to -- dress when you were walking around the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from the white rag that we had to have on our left arms, there were no other requirements.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm interested in the white rag. Can you please explain to the Chamber what precisely that requirement was and who it applied to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a requirement that was designed to distinguish the non-Serb population from the Serb population so it applied to Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Again, how did you become aware of that requirement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the requirement to put this kind of insignia, so to speak? I saw a [redacted], Djoko Pisarevic, [redacted] , he was standing outside my window and he told me that we were all to put the white rags.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: At the time that he explained that, did he say anything about it applying to Croats or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not, but he, himself, did not wear this white rag because he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Following you becoming aware of the requirement to wear the white rag, did you actually see people about the town wearing such a white rag or ribbon or whatever it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The people that you saw wearing the white rag and white ribbon, what ethnic group did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I want to turn now to your arrest, please. Can you just remind the Chamber of when you were arrested. If you can't remember the date, try and give us a fix on which month it was in which you were arrested.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Had you been to perform labour duties prior to your arrest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Tell us how it was that you came to be arrested, what happened at the actual time of your arrest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not go to work on that day. I was ill and I was unable to go to work. The next day, the police came to get me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who was it who came to get you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djoko Maslic and Pero Krstanovic, the Serb police officers. MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry, would Your Honours please bear with me. I just need to check something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You mentioned a gentleman named Krstanovic the other day when you were giving evidence in respect of the events relating to the mosque. What I want to know is whether that person that you mentioned the other day is the same person who came to arrest you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not the same person. The person that is connected with the mosque incident is Perica, and I spoke about Pero Krstanovic in relation to the events in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Baen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in light of everything that's pending before the Court right now, we respectfully request that the Prosecution not seek to elicit anything about the mosque or any religious property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Those instructions were given to the Prosecution yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: He just mentioned it there. MR. DI FAZIO: I can allay the fears of the Defence. I'm not interested in the mosque at all, I'm just making sure that the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The difference of the persons, and I'm sure reasonableness would just show that it's just in relation to explaining that the two people are different.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Just for the purposes of the record, we just object what he to what he asked in line 15, page 7. Thank you, Your Honour. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, you told us that those two gentlemen came to arrest you and where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the police station in Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Baen, I just want to -- you have said that you object to the answer elicited in line -- the question in line 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, 15, line 15. Well, it's lines 14 and 15, but the language relating to the mosque is in line 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but it doesn't mean anything, just to say "relating to the mosque."

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: He said -- he's asking him about the events we talked about earlier in your testimony relating to the mosque. Your Honour, I'm not trying to make a big deal here I'm just trying to be careful for the purposes of record until this issue of the amended indictment is resolved. That's all, Your Honour. I'm just trying to make the record clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the SUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 27th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to now ask you some questions about the period of time which you spent in the SUP up until late November 1992. In that period of time, were you beaten whilst inside the SUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So you were in the SUP for over two months, I think. Can you give the Chamber an idea of how often you personally were beaten whilst you were in custody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every two or three days, depending on the mood of the Serb police officers. If they lost at cards, they would come there drunk and they would beat us. So they beat us quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just one further matter. You say that you were beaten by the Serb police officers. Were these men locals or were they from elsewhere in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people from the areas of former Yugoslavia, but the people who beat us more frequently were the locals.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the period of time in which you stayed in the SUP, were you kept in the one location within the SUP or were you moved around from place to place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was kept in one and the same location.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: With the permission of the Trial Chamber, and if it's okay with you, I would like you to look, very, very briefly, at one photograph. That's all that I want to do, and I won't dwell upon that. Perhaps, Witness, you could tell us if that would hurt your eyes to do that. Are you up to, very briefly, looking at a photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Perhaps you can deal with that maybe next year -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- after a long break. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I won't trouble you with that at the moment, Witness. Tell us this: The room in which you were kept in the SUP, did you have a view out into the street, the street that runs between the SUP and the TO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How many people were kept in that room with you in the SUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number would change quite often: 7, 8, 11. That was the biggest number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What sort of food were you provided with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: A piece of bread with some jam spread on it, or perhaps some lard, and that would last us 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber how often you received a meal per day? I want to know what you had --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just once.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you hungry in the time that you were in the SUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just returning briefly to the numbers who were incarcerated with you in that room, you said the numbers fluctuated between 7 and 11. What sort of space did you have in the room? And I suppose in telling us, you ought to give us an idea of the proportions of the room in which 7 to 11 men were kept.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four by three. That's 12 square metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was there enough room for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What about sleeping conditions? Were you provided with anything to sleep on, anything to cover yourself and keep yourself warm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We slept on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber if it was safe for you to go to the lavatory when you needed to when you were in the --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber why that was so.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because very often we were beaten in the toilets, so we were afraid to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What was the age of the people who were incarcerated along with you in that room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were quite a few elderly people aged between 60 and 65. I was about the youngest person there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did any of them provide you, that is, your fellow prisoners, provide you with any explanation as to why they had been arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marko Saric [Realtime transcript read in error "Sadic"], from Hasici, age 65, was arrested because they had established in some way or another that he was an Ustasha scout, and he had remained in his village, and that's where they found him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the time that you were in the SUP, incarcerated there, were you ever interviewed by any official, judge or magistrate or police officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Before you proceed, can we just have clarification to the previous answer. When he says, in reference to Hasic [phoen], who was aged 65, they had established in some way or another that he was who, the "they"? MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Perhaps you can give us some further information, if you have it, regarding Mr. Marko Saric from Hasici. The Tribunal wants to know - sorry - the Chamber wants to know who it was that had established that he was an Ustasha scout. Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the policeman who established that, led by investigator Milos Savic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did this gentleman, Mr. Marko Saric [Realtime transcript read in error "Savic"], ever say anything to you that indicated whether or not he accepted that he was an Ustasha scout? In other words, did he say something to show that he was in fact an Ustasha scout, or did he deny it or comment upon it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Hasici fell, he hid in his own house, together with Pavo Dragicevic, aged 67. Those are all the men who didn't want to leave their homes. So in a raid that followed, the Serb police arrested them and brought them to the police station, where they were kept in the same room with me. He never mentioned anything except that he had indeed had a rifle. But they were old men. They were not fit for that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the purposes of the clarification on the record, speaking about this event, we have several versions of the family name of this person from the village of Hasici. For example, page 12, line 17, it mentioned that it's Marko Savic, and then on the other occasions it's Marko Sadic. But I believe that it's obviously complicated for the speakers not knowing our language. The witness said Marko Saric, S-a-r-i-c, so finally we have four versions. So please, if you may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the correct name of this old man aged about 65 detained in the same room with Witness M. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Witness, you've been referring to a gentleman whose first name is Marko just recently in your evidence. Can you give us a clear indication of what you understand his surname to be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marko Saric, S-a-r-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I was going to ask you about your own interview. I think you said that you were interviewed yourself, and I don't want to misquote you but I think you also said that it was Mr. Milos Savic who interviewed you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: About how long after you were first arrested were you interviewed and where were you interviewed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: This interview took place on the upper floor of the police station and it was maybe ten days after I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who was present when you were interviewed apart from yourself and Mr. Savic or was that all, were there only two persons in the room during the course of the interview?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another policeman whose name I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: By this stage, had you been beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the beatings that you had received up until this point, the point that you were interviewed, had instruments been used by those who were beating you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police truncheon was often used plus punching and kicking. They usually punched us and kicked us and sometimes used the truncheon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what appearance you would have presented to Mr. Milos Savic at the time that you were interviewed by him, and I'm referring to, in particular, any sign of injury?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had injuries to my face, wounds. I don't even know what to call them properly, bleeding wounds. Blood had just stopped flowing before I went to see him to be interviewed, the day before, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were your clothes encrusted with blood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, in the course of the interview with Mr. Savic, was it ever explained to you what it was that you were accused of doing or suspected of doing or were you ever provided with a reason as to why you had been arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milos Savic just showed me a piece of paper with my name and surname written on it indicating that I was a scout. I didn't see or wasn't shown anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And the fact of you being a scout and your name being on this piece of paper, was that the central issue in which he was interested in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. di Fazio, will you be asking the witness what exactly a scout was supposed to have done? MR. DI FAZIO: I'll try and clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You heard Her Honour's question. Can you tell us, did they ever actually say to you or explain to you what a scout was and what precisely you had been doing as a scout to warrant this arrest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not quite clear to me to this day what I was supposed to do, what I could have done, and what sort of task I could have had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Just a clarification there. You earlier said that Marko Saric was said to be a Ustasha scout. What about yourself? When you saw that piece of paper, did it describe what sort of a scout you were; a Croatian scout, a Ustasha scout, or just a scout?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw that I was a reserve scout, and weighing 135 kilos that I weighed at the time, I don't know what kind of scout I would have made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: And by "reserve," you understood it to mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you it's not clear to me to this day this definition of reserve scout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we are now at the level of so-called spirit of language. My understanding of term scout is that this activity pertained to younger children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. You are not going to give evidence. The witness is the one explaining that he is the one who was told that he was a scout.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I agree absolutely, but just to clarification, whether the use of term scout is using in the military notion, as a military notion. I don't know. I'm not familiar with this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, if you will remember your civil war in America, the army had army scouts. MR. DI FAZIO: I don't think anyone is under any illusion that we are talking about boy scouts here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That was my suspicion, you know, but maybe in terms of the translations, if you are referring to army scout, that's more precise, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But that is a matter for the Prosecution to deal with and the witness to explain if he understood anything by it. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was it ever explained to you who you were a scout for, for which group or organisation or ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's very simple. They said I was a scout of Alija's, meaning Alija the President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you ever provided with any detail as to the sort of scouting activities that you had apparently engaged in? Did Mr. Milos Savic ever say to you you were scouting here or there and carrying a weapon when you were doing so, that sort of detail that would enlighten you, give you an idea of what it was you were supposed to have done as a scout?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milos Savic just kept holding his truncheon and beating it against the desk and telling me, "Come on, talk." And I never got any explanation what kind of scout I was supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like you to answer my next question, if you may, with just a yes or a no. Do you know a gentleman named Stevo Arandjic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Think back. Was his name ever mentioned during the course of this interview? I'm talking about the interview or interrogation with Milos Savic. That's all I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever seek any explanation as to why you should be arrested in September for carrying out scouting activities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was arrested, I was told that I was being taken for an interview, but I never got an explanation as to why I had been arrested in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did Mr. Savic ever give you an explanation of when it was that you had conducted these scouting activities, alleged scouting activities? For instance, did he say it was in April, before the takeover or that you had been engaged in scouting activities at night after you'd finished your labour duties, anything like that as to give you an idea of when it was that you were supposed to have done this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Following the interview, did you sign any statement or put your signature on any piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I want to return now to the conditions that you endured in the SUP. In the period of time that you were incarcerated there, did any of the prisoners in your room have their teeth pulled out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, undergo that experience?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who pulled your teeth out, how did they do it, and when did they do it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slavko Trifunovic, nicknamed accordionist, used to pull people's teeth out. He would put on a white doctor's coat and a dentist's pliers. He pretended he was a dentist. It was a sort of play acting, and he would pull people's teeth out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Apart from this torture that he engaged in, did he have some sort of official role at the SUP, for example, did he -- was a policeman there or a guard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: A local policeman, that is, someone from the -- in the area of Bosanski Samac or the municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How many of your teeth were pulled out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber exactly how it transpired, how it started, what happened when he came into the room, and in as much detail as you can recall.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he would come into the room, we all had to get up, stand at attention, and bend. First, he would start hitting us with a truncheon to calm us down, and then he would start pulling our teeth. He wasn't picky. He didn't spare anyone. He didn't choose young or old people, in particular. He would do it to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you have to be held down or did others hold you as he did this? How did he -- I just don't understand how he actually executed the motion.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: You weren't allowed to move. Nobody held me. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I want to ask the witness about a number of matters now that involve allegations of sexual mistreatment. It might be appropriate, I think, to protect any names of any victims and for us to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I would like you to comment upon how loud the yells and screams were. Can you give us an idea?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they beat a person, the rest of us had to sing in order for the screams not to be heard and for the other sounds not to be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were there ever occasions when you weren't singing and men were yelling and screaming?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, on those occasions, can you tell us how loud those yells and screams were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how loud it was on the outside, but as for us in the room, we could hear very loud screams, moans, cries.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What sort of songs were you forced to sing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chetnik songs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you ever required to stand for long periods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How did that affect the older men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would fall down. They just couldn't take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What sort of period of time are we talking about when you say that men were forced to stand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would depend. At one point they would take pity on us, but on some occasions we would have to stand for maybe four or five hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thus far, you've described only men being incarcerated in the SUP, can you tell us if any women were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two women held upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know who they were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the full name of one of them and as for the other, I know that she worked at the department store. The first one is Bejka Barjaktarevic. She was in her 50s. According to their papers, she was a sniper. The other woman was from Gradacac. She worked in the Bosanski Samac department store, and apparently or allegedly she had picked up some goods in Samac and tried to escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What was the ethnic background of these women as far as you were aware?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both of them were Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How do you know that the allegation against one of them was that she was a sniper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because Milos Savic told me that they knew everything, and he said that they had caught Bejka who was a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How old was this woman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 50 years of age. I don't know exactly, but that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you have any idea if they were mistreated in any way or is it the case that you don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you eventually transferred away from the SUP in late November?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the camp in Batkovici near Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How many of you went from Bosanski Samac to Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 180.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were these all Bosanski Samac men or at least from the municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were people from the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How long did you end up remaining in Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June 1994, I was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What -- where were you kept in Batkovici, what sort of place was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a large hangar, 60 by 30 metres, I think. This is where they used to keep grain since this used to be a farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the time that you were there, did you perform any labour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber what sort of work you were doing whilst you were being held at Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had to work on the farm. We had to do work with corn and soy beans.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what about the general conditions that you saw at Batkovici compared to the SUP, and I'm thinking now in terms of your sleeping, the food, being able to go to the lavatory, beatings, that sort of thing. Can you just give the Chamber a picture of conditions in Batkovici and the way in which they differed, if any, from the SUP in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conditions in Batkovici were better than in Bosanski Samac. We had greater freedom of movement, we had all the water that we wanted. We had three meals a day. The only thing is that we had to work more. That was actually the big difference. And as regards the sleeping facilities, the situation was the same because we had to sleep on the concrete floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you have blankets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were registered on the 3rd of December, the Red Cross brought some.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you register with the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This is the 3rd of December, 1993, the registration with the Red Cross, because it says they were registered on 3rd December. What year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992, 3rd of December. That is when we were registered. MR. DI FAZIO: Does that clarify the matter for Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: When did they move to Batkovici? MR. DI FAZIO: In late 1992, in November -- sorry, late November 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So in December 1992, they -- MR. DI FAZIO: Were registered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Registered by the Red Cross. MR. DI FAZIO: That's right. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. di Fazio, could you clarify whether this is the International Committee of the Red Cross or whether this was the Red Cross of the former Yugoslavia. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you hear Her Honour's question? Have you got any idea at all when you say that you were registered whether it was the worldwide International Red Cross or whether it was the Red Cross of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How did that assist you if, indeed, it did in Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were given cards and murders could no longer take place. We would be given food that they would bring in from time to time and they would visit us every ten days and then we would be given a pack of cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Are you saying it was the International Red Cross that brought the food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What about communication with the outside world? Perhaps I should be more specific. Did the fact of your registration with the International Red Cross assist communication with the outside world? I mean by that letters or phone calls, anything like that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How did it assist?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would bring us some message forms and pens and we would then be able to write any messages we wanted and the International Red Cross would then forward these messages for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Once you'd finished using the pens, what would happen to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once the Red Cross was gone, the duty police officer in the camp would collect all the pens.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the period of time that you were in Batkovici, did beatings occur from time to time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you personally beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guards did it, the police officers there that guarded us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How often were you beaten in Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: They beat us right at the beginning, but when they realised that we were unable to work if we were beaten up, then they stopped. So after a month, there were no more beatings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was there ever collective punishment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Explain to the Chamber what you saw -- you saw happen when collective punishment took place.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: If somebody tried to escape or if somebody came drunk from the work place, then we all had to stand between 8 and 10 hours in the snow or in the rain and we had to stand at attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How often did instances of collective punishment occur that you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the time that you were at Batkovici, were you placed on trial?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I seek to tender into evidence two documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: -- that relate to this witness and the trial. A draft translation has been prepared for that, and I would ask that that only be given an ID number. The full translation, or official translation, should not take too long, and I would at a later point seek to introduce into evidence, completely into evidence the full and official translation. But I would ask at this stage that the draft only be given an identification number, because I don't propose to seek its full admission when I intend to use the official translation at a later point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Why don't we just have -- the document you have is in Serbo-Croat? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Why can't we just have that as ID, and then, when the full translation comes, we have both of them admitted? MR. DI FAZIO: We can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: There will be no objection. MR. DI FAZIO: If we can, I'm happy to do that. It's just that if I do that, then Your Honours won't have something to look at in the -- when I'm eliciting evidence of this from the defendant. I'm quite happy to approach it in that fashion. I'm only concerned that Your Honours have something, at least, to look at when I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Unless you want to have certain parts of that document read out. Because, you see, it causes confusion when you have the draft translation marked and utilised and then you have the full translation come into the record. It does cause confusion in the event that the two versions differ, and it's clumsy for the Trial Chamber to use two versions, because that's what we'll do in the end. MR. DI FAZIO: Very well, Your Honours. I will not seek to admit into -- have marked the draft translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And perhaps this is one other item you can skip and deal with it later, when you have the full translation, that is, if you tend to discuss the contents of the documents. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, we could do that. I hadn't thought of that, frankly. That might, in fact, be the easiest method, and we can just skip this whole --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This part, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: This part, and I can deal with what remains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: In that case, I won't have too much more material for this morning, but -- we'll go past 11.30, but not long beyond that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That is okay, but it's important to have a record which makes sense. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Very well. I'm grateful for that. With respect, it's a practical solution to my dilemma. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. di Fazio, I'm wondering if you can clarify from

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By the time he left SUP, what sort of injuries had he suffered, the extent; and 2) whether he had any access to doctors at the SUP. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Witness, the Chamber wishes to know what sort of injuries you had suffered by the time you eventually came to leave the SUP. Now, we know that obviously you had suffered injuries to your jaw, I suppose, and your teeth, because they had been pulled. But can you tell us anything else, if there were any other injuries, what those injuries were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: My nose was broken, the bones inside my nose, and that also happened in SUP, in addition to the injuries I had sustained earlier when I had been beaten. As far as medical care is concerned, we had none. Dr. Ozren Stanimirovic would come from time to time. When we were totally exhausted from hunger, he would laugh and say, "Don't eat too much, because you seem to have overeaten."

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I see. So who was this Dr. Stanimirovic? Where was -- firstly, what was his ethnic background and where did he come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came to Samac from Serbia. He worked there as a doctor. And he is of Serbian ethnic background, of Orthodox faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Was he working in Bosanski Samac as a doctor prior to the events of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can I seek clarification? Is it your evidence, Witness, that this doctor, who was known to be a medical doctor by the witness, would just come in and simply say what the witness has said, without ever treating any of the prisoners? MR. DI FAZIO: I'm going to explore what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber, first of all, how often he would visit whilst you were incarcerated in the SUP between September and late November.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one of the prisoners got sick, then he would be called and he would arrive, but I had never seen him offer any medical assistance to anyone, give any kind of tablets or anything, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What about when you had your teeth pulled? Did he come along and give you any medical treatment for that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What about when you had your nose broken? Did he treat you for that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So what precisely did he do when he turned up at the SUP? You've told us what he didn't do, but what did he do? Did he actually look at the prisoners, examine them, ask them questions about their injuries, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would act in a very ironic manner and he would laugh. He may have helped some of the prisoners whose lives may have been in danger, but he would simply be there -- it would be a token gesture: Well, a doctor has come. But he never did anything, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever see him bandage anyone, give anyone an injection, give anyone some pills, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: It may be difficult for you, but if you can tell us, how often did he visit or did you see him at the SUP between September and late November 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him quite often, because people were exhausted from hunger and they would be fainting. He would come, pour some water on the prisoner who had fainted, and then he would leave. That was the extent of his medical treatment, of Dr. Stanimirovic's medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know who arranged for him to be taken to the SUP? Was it the entreaties of prisoners or was it just a fact that he turned up and that was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty police officer called him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me? I just want to make sure I've covered the issues raised by Your Honour Judge Singh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Does that evidence clarify the issues that Your Honour wished to have raised? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you receive any medical treatment while you were in Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we reported to the duty officer, he would take us to see a doctor in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And was that real medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you compare it to the situation in Samac, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I'm going to move on to another topic. Do you want me to start that now? It's only two minutes to 11.00. I prefer to deal with it at the one time, and I will definitely finish as far as I can go this morning, but we're going to inevitably go to 11.30 and I will probably wrap up as far as I can go today soon after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I just want to clarify with the witness the medical treatment in Batkovici where he used to be taken in town to the doctors. Is it correct to say that whilst in Batkovici, you were treated for all your injuries and you did recover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Can I just clarify one aspect of that answer, if Your Honours please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because we've still got two minutes. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You said that you recovered. Was that because you got medical treatment for the broken nose and for the teeth and so on? Did you actually go and see a doctor and get treatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I did not receive any medical treatment for that. I recovered from these injuries on my own, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, receive any medical treatment in Batkovici or are you reporting what you saw of -- happen to others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw what happened to the others and also, as far as I was concerned, because I got diabetes, I was taken to have my sugar level checked and I also received medication, some pills for the diabetes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And was it -- did you see doctors in Batkovici only in relation to your diabetes or to other injuries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: And also for other injuries. If, for instance, you had been beaten up. And often, a doctor came to see us in the hangar since Dr. Stanko Pivasevic worked in Bijeljina and he was originally from Samac, he would quite often come personally to the hangar to bring us medication.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what was his bedside manner like compared to that of Dr. -- the other doctor who treated you in Bosanski Samac? How did he treat the prisoners, in other words?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: He treated us very nicely and he really tried to help everyone. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a break and resume our proceedings at 1130 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we will continue with the Prosecution. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours. Just before I ask the next question, I will let the Chamber know that further from the matters raised by my learned friend Mr. Weiner this morning, the Defence have now been provided with a document which sets out the possible options the Prosecution will pursue in respect to the wording of the indictment and, in particular, in respect to the wording "wanton" and "extensive." They've been -- the document clearly sets out those options. They have those. And so by noon on Monday, the Prosecution will make clear to them which of those options it will pursue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yeah. Those are consultations between the parties. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I just merely wanted to place on the record that they have been informed in writing of those options. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Witness, before the break we were talking about your period of time in Batkovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. di Fazio, I wonder whether, before you go on to the next question, whether you could clarify with the witness: He's mentioned that he had diabetes. Did he have knowledge that he had diabetes before his incarceration? That might be useful for us to know. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell the Chamber if your diabetes, for which you received treatment whilst in Batkovici, was a condition that you became aware of whilst you were there, or was it a condition of some longstanding, something that you had suffered from prior to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about that while I was at Batkovici. I didn't have it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And was it regulated by changes in diet, or did you have insulin injections or any other treatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received tablets at the hospital in Bijeljina, and that's where I had check-ups for my sugar level.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And in the period of time you were in Batkovici, which is about 18 to 19 months, or thereabouts, how often did you receive treatment for your diabetes at the hospital in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only when I would run out of tablets, then I would go to be issued with a new package.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you if in the time that you were at Batkovici, if you saw any of the defendants in the hangar or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only during an exchange, I would then see Mr. Miroslav Tadic, who came with a list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Approximately how many occasions did you see him at Batkovici with these lists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell you precisely, but I saw him about five or six times.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: On each of those occasions, did he have lists in his possession?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: On each of those occasions, and following his visits, were prisoners who were in the hangar taken away to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you anxious to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was hoping that I would return home. I wasn't looking forward to leaving to someone else what it had taken me 20 years to acquire. But later I realised that there would be -- it wouldn't be possible to continue living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever have an opportunity of speaking to Miroslav Tadic about an exchange?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only once. I asked him about it, and he told me, "You should return to Samac, because we need craftsmen."

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What did you say to him on this occasion? Did you have a request for him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no request, and I prayed to God that I wouldn't be returned to Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, how was it that he came to say to you that you should return to Samac because we need craftsmen? How was it that he came up with an answer like that? What I'm interested in is, was it preceded by any question or a request from you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of my colleagues who had worked in the waterworks in Samac had all been detained, from director to the janitor. We were all at the camp in Batkovici. So there were no plumbers left in Samac, and that's probably what Mr. Tadic had in mind when he was saying this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were any of those same men who were from the waterworks and who were detained with you in Batkovici, were any of them kept in institutions in - I won't say institutions - were any of them kept in the TO or the SUP in Bosanski Samac in the time that you were incarcerated there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: About how many of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: there were seven or eight of us who had been employed with the waterworks. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me. I just want to look at the transcript in a little more detail, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When Mr. Tadic said to you that you should return, that you should return to Bosanski Samac because craftsmen were needed, what was your response?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly what I replied, but I know I wasn't overjoyed at the idea of going back.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was there any cost involved in getting exchanged as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: So far as I know, when I was exchanged, there were no costs involved when I was exchanged between the Bosnian side and the army of the Republika Srpska. And everybody in Samac told me, however, that they had paid to be put on the exchange list, however, I never saw a price list or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So you're now telling the Chamber for matters that were reported to you regarding the question of cost. What I want to know is whether, in these matters that were reported to you, were you ever told to whom payments would have to be made to be placed on the exchange list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the wife of Avdo Drljacic said she had paid 400 Deutschmark to Miroslav Tadic to put Avdo on the list, and that's how Avdo finally got exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman or a person named Sabah Seric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss with him the question of cost of exchanges?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since he was detained together with me at Batkovici, he told me that he had asked Mr. Tadic once and Tadic told him to get ready and that once he had the money, he would be put on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did that gentleman ever report actually having paid money?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't tell me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When were you eventually taken through the process known as an exchange?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 2nd of June, 1994, I was exchanged in Sutorovici, Tuzla municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Is that Sutorovici, is that a small village or town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a small village, medium-sized village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How far from Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How were you taken from Batkovici to this small village of Sutorovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 18 of us who were exchanged then. We went to town on a military truck. There, we boarded a bus and then we waited for enough civilians to gather to fill the bus and then they took us to the separation line at Sutorovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So the bus carried with it, on board it, I should say, a number of prisoners plus civilians who were picked up as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who was the ethnic background of both the prisoners and the civilians that the bus picked up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were exclusively Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Approximately how many were on the bus and furthermore, was there only one bus that was involved in this exchange?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only one bus and about 50 of us were exchanged, 18 from Batkovici and another 30 from the town of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were they all, as far as you could tell, Bosnians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Into whose custody or territory were you placed once the exchange was completed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were handed over to the BH army, to the soldiers, because we were on their territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The people who were on the bus, did it include women and children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did it include elderly men and women?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did it include, as far as you could tell, combatants, soldiers, military types?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Once you had passed into the control of the soldiers of the BH army, what did they do with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took us to collective accommodation in the Mejdan hall in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I don't think I've asked you for the date of your exchange. Can you tell us the date or -- that this event occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd of June, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Had your wife undergone the process known as exchange prior to your being exchanged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did she take your children with her?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you eventually reunited?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When were you reunited, where were you reunited, and under whose control was the territory were you were reunited?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was reunited with my family in July of 1994 in Orasje. Orasje was controlled by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When your wife was exchanged and took the children with her, was she able to take with her any of the property that you and she had owned in your former life prior to April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just her personal belongings and the personal belongings of our children.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, was that carried in bags?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Have you ever heard from her how many bags she was able to take with her when she left Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since our children were quite small, she could only carry one bag and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What sort of possessions did she have with her when you were reunited with her in Orasje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: She rented an apartment. She had to pay the rent, and she didn't have any of her personal property because she had to leave everything behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, in June 1994, you were exchanged. Did you have any input in any way at all as to the decision of when to exchange you, and the fact that you were being exchanged? In other words, were you ever consulted or asked about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody ever asked me about that. Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When did you first learn that you were to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening of the 1st. In the evening they read out the list of names so that we could get ready by morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Had you even known before the 1st of June that anyone was considering exchanging you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In April of 1992, had you any plans or intention or desire to uproot yourself from Bosanski Samac and take up life elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I assume that your apartment, prior to the 16th and 17th of April, 1992, had your furniture and your possessions and your memorabilia of your past life. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever see any of that stuff again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you -- or rather, have you made any moves to regain possession or some sort of control over your apartment? I mean, of course, the apartment in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did get my apartment back, but it's been completely emptied out, so there's no way I can go back to Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Are you planning to renovate it and clean it up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards my apartment, I cleaned that up and now I'm waiting for the possibility to arise for me to be able to buy it from the state, and then I intend to sell it to somebody, because I have no intention of living there, in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Sorry. What do you mean by "buy it back from the state"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the current procedure. Since I had been given my apartment from my company that I worked for, it was considered to be publicly owned. Now I have to invest some money in it, and then I will be entitled to the full ownership of this apartment and I will be able to buy it from the state, and then I will be able to sell it to a third party. That's the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: If the events in April of 1992 had not occurred, would you have had the right to continue residing in that apartment throughout all these years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Would you have had the right to rent out the apartment and get rent for it, keep the rent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, I would have had the right to rent the apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Have you ever received any income generated from your apartment between April of 1992 and now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean, but since it is my intention to sell it, and since I do have a prospective buyer who has offered me a price of 2.000 German marks for the apartment -- in fact, it's an advance payment, these 2.000 German marks, and once I complete the purchase from the state, then I will get the rest of the sum from the buyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I was wondering about your questions on whether or not he was getting rent at any time, because he had explained, when Judge Singh asked him, that the apartment was owned by the company he was working for, it was allocated to him, so it was considered publicly owned. MR. DI FAZIO: I appreciate that, but I just don't know, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: He wasn't -- he was not -- the witness -- to my understanding, the witness was not the registered owner. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I heard that and understood that, if Your Honours please. I don't know what the system is in Yugoslavia, and therefore, I don't know if that means that he's got the right to rent it and generate income. The state of the evidence is that he -- at this stage is that he says he does have that right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: After buying it from the state he will have that right. MR. DI FAZIO: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: And at most, he may have had the right to sublease it, provided that his lease from the state entitled him to sublease it. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I would be happy if I can help my learned colleague with these details, but of course -- if we are entering into this topic, maybe it would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- useful. No, no. Of course, I'm not intending to cross-examine this witness about that. He's a layperson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Not even to give evidence yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: He's a layperson, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Not even to give evidence yourself. Yes. If the Prosecution are intending to have any issue at all, it is their duty to clarify that with the witness. If they are satisfied with the situation as it is, that is fine. When the Defence comes on with the opportunity to cross-examine, they can also get their own version from the witness if they so wish. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I'd just like to clarify it, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Witness, what I'm concerned about is this: I just want to know what the situation is, and do your best to assist the Chamber. You said, have said, that the apartment was owned by the state and that, at this stage, at least, you still need to buy it in order to sell it. What I'm concerned about is the period of time when presumably the state still owned the apartment, that is, after your arrest and continuing up until this day. Now, in that situation, where the state is in fact the owner of the apartment, are you permitted, or would you have been permitted, to leave the apartment, rent it out, collect the rents?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours. Calling for speculation. This person cannot give the right answer. And in addition, he stated that probably there would be some possibilities in previous answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought that the question is trying to deal with the right of ownership. Yes, it does sound like asking him to speculate. I thought the Prosecution was trying to find out what type of ownership he enjoyed. MR. DI FAZIO: And rights of ownership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, what right of ownership he enjoyed vis-a-vis the state, the office where he was working which allocated the apartment to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Page 47, line 8 and 9. The part of -- finally, the question of my learned colleague was: "Now, in that situation, where the state is, in fact, the owner of the apartment, are you permitted, or would you have been permitted, to leave the apartment, rent it out, collect the rents?" I mean, that's obvious. Our own colleague tried to establish the situation in hypothetical terms. So that was the basis of my reaction, nothing more. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm trying to establish an intensely practical thing, and I don't see that asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought so. MR. DI FAZIO: And I don't see that asking someone, "Are you allowed to rent out your house, your apartment?" is an invitation to speculation. Who better than this person to tell us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because it would depend on how he understands his right of ownership to be, to have been at the time. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, exactly. It's a matter that he can talk about. I mean we all know if we can rent out our house or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So he can go ahead and answer that question. MR. DI FAZIO: May I just have a moment to confer with my colleague, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you -- I'll just repeat my question to you briefly. It concerns the period of time between April 1992 and up to the present. You've told us that the state owned the apartment. What I want to know is: In that period of time, if you had wanted to rent out the apartment, could you have done so, would you have been permitted to do so, and if so, would you have been permitted to pocket the rent generated? That's all I want to know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my state, Bosnia, there is rights, a law governing the right of a tenant. If you spend ten years in an apartment owned by your company or by the state, you are considered to be a co-owner of that apartment which entitled you to either rent that apartment or to sell it if you want to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: So basically you have possession with the option to purchase it after ten years. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How long had you been in the apartment or owned -- possessed the apartment, I should say, been in possession of the apartment as at April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1975, which means 17 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: I have one question there, please. Any reason why, after ten years, you had not decided to purchase it earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That law had not been enforced yet at that time and, in fact, it is not in force yet in the Republika Srpska and it will probably be enacted in January next year, and this was the only thing that prevented me from actually buying my apartment. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How did you actually go about the process of recovering possession of your apartment and cleaning it out and getting it into saleable form?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Actually, that doesn't matter because he has already stated that he has an accrued right to purchase it, so it's an accrued right there. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I'm not so concerned about that issue, if Your Honour pleases.
